name: Dublin
info: Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland, on Dublin Bay at the mouth of the River Liffey, a Viking foundation of about 841 that became the seat of English power in Ireland and, in 1922, of the Irish Free State.

facts.founded: A Viking settlement of about 841 called Dyflin, beside a Christian ecclesiastical settlement known as Duibhlinn; a Gaelic settlement, Áth Cliath, stood further up the river. The Irish government recognised 988 as the year of the city's settlement.
facts.where: On Dublin Bay at the mouth of the River Liffey in the province of Leinster, on the east coast of Ireland, with the Dublin Mountains to the south.
facts.known: The Viking town of Dyflin; Dublin Castle, founded in 1204; Trinity College, founded in 1592; Georgian Dublin and the Wide Streets Commission; the Parliament of Ireland until 1800; the Easter Rising of 1916; the Guinness brewery; the capital of the Irish Free State
facts.today: Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland and the seat of its parliament, the Oireachtas.

t: The Vikings established a fortified base at Dublin in 841, and the town grew into a commercial centre that stayed largely under Viking control until the Norman invasion launched from Wales in 1169.
Dublin Castle, founded in 1204, made the city the centre of Anglo-Norman and then English power in Ireland, and in the 18th century the city was rebuilt with wide Georgian streets and squares.

The Act of Union of 1800 ended the Parliament of Ireland in Dublin, and after the Easter Rising of 1916, the War of Independence and the Civil War the city became the capital of the Irish Free State in 1922.
dyk: Dublin's name comes from the Irish Duiblinn, "black pool", a dark tidal pool where the River Poddle entered the Liffey, on the site of the castle gardens at the rear of Dublin Castle.
ev: The Vikings establish a fortified base at Dublin
The Irish High King Brian Boru defeats the Norse at the Battle of Clontarf

sections.origins:
Humans have lived around Dublin Bay since prehistoric times. Fish traps found during the building of the Convention Centre Dublin point to habitation as far back as 6,000 years ago, and further traps near St James's Gate indicate Mesolithic activity. Ptolemy's map of Ireland, of about 140 CE, has been read as the earliest reference to a settlement near Dublin, a place he called Eblana, but doubt has since been cast on the identification, and the similarity of the names is now thought to be coincidental.

The name Dublin comes from the Middle Irish Duiblinn, "black pool", the name of a dark tidal pool where the River Poddle entered the Liffey, on the site of the castle gardens. A Christian ecclesiastical settlement known as Duibhlinn stood there before the Vikings, and the Viking settlement of about 841, Dyflin, took its name from it. Evidence from a dig in Temple Bar suggests that Anglo-Saxons occupied Dublin before the Vikings arrived. From the 9th and 10th centuries two settlements lay where the modern city stands: the Scandinavian one on the Poddle, in the area now called Wood Quay, and the Gaelic Áth Cliath, "ford of hurdles", further up the Liffey near the present Father Mathew Bridge. Its name is still the basis of the Irish name of the city, Baile Átha Cliath. The Irish government recognised 988 as the year in which the city was settled, and Dublin celebrated its millennium in 1988.
sections.growth:
In 841 the Vikings established a fortified base at Dublin. The town grew into a substantial commercial centre under Olaf Guthfrithson in the mid-to-late 10th century. According to some historians, part of its early economic growth came from the slave trade, which reached its height in Ireland and Dublin in the 9th and 10th centuries; Viking Dublin had a large slave market, and captives from Wales, England, Normandy and beyond were sold there. The Thingmote, a raised mound where the Norsemen assembled and made their laws, stood on the south side of the river beside the later castle until 1685.

After the Norman conquest Dublin prospered as a trade centre. The appointment of the first Lord Mayor in 1229 was followed by growth, and the city had a population of 8,000 by the end of the 13th century. Dublin then remained a relatively small walled medieval town. After the plague of 1649 to 1651 the city prospered again through the wool and linen trade with England, reaching a population of over 50,000 by 1700, and by 1698 the manufacture of wool employed 12,000 people. In the 18th century the Wide Streets Commission, established in 1757, governed the layout of streets, bridges and buildings. Guinness began brewing at St James's Gate in 1759, and linen exports rose from over 1.5 million yards in 1710 to almost 19 million yards by 1779. By 1814 the population was 175,319, and 233,159 in 1841.
sections.rulers:
The Vikings ruled Dublin for almost three centuries, though they were expelled in 902 and returned in 917, and the town remained largely under Viking control until 1169. After the death of Muirchertach Mac Lochlainn in early 1166, Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair, King of Connacht, went to Dublin and was inaugurated King of Ireland without opposition. Diarmait Mac Murchada, King of Leinster, who had been exiled by Ruaidrí, enlisted Strongbow, the Earl of Pembroke, to conquer Dublin, and Strongbow declared himself King of Leinster after gaining control of the city. Henry II of England mounted a larger invasion in 1171 and pronounced himself Lord of Ireland. Dublin became the capital of the English Lordship of Ireland, established in 1177.

The city was the heart of the Pale, a narrow strip of English settlement along the east coast. The Tudor conquest of the 16th century gave it new prominence as the centre of administration, and it was the capital of the Lordship of Ireland from 1171 to 1541 and of the Kingdom of Ireland from 1541 to 1800. The Parliament of Ireland had met in the city from 1297. After the Act of Union Dublin was part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland from 1801 to 1922. The Irish Republic of 1919 to 1922 also had its capital there, and in 1922 Dublin became the capital of the Irish Free State, renamed Ireland in 1937.
sections.life:
Medieval Dublin was a small place of around 5,000 to 10,000 people, an enclave of no more than three square kilometres hugging the south side of the Liffey. Outside the walls lay suburbs such as the Liberties, on the lands of the Archbishop of Dublin, and Irishtown, where Gaelic Irish were supposed to live after a 15th-century law expelled them from the city. After the Anglo-Normans took Dublin in 1171, many of the Norse inhabitants built their own settlement on the north side, known as Ostmantown or Oxmantown. The city was traditionally one of two languages, English and Irish. A 16th-century English administrator, William Gerard, wrote that even in Dublin most people spoke Irish, and Irish scribes and poets worked in the city through the 18th century.

Faith divided the city. Elizabeth I founded Trinity College in 1592 as a Protestant university and ordered the Catholic St Patrick's and Christ Church cathedrals to be converted to the Protestant church. Protestants became a majority in Dublin in the 1640s, and Catholics became the majority again in the late 18th century. In the Georgian city the Wide Streets Commission replaced narrow medieval streets with large streets, among them Sackville Street, now O'Connell Street, and five major squares were laid out. Handel's Messiah was first performed on Fishamble Street in 1742. The 18th-century city also had a growing slum population, and rival gangs, the Protestant Liberty Boys and the Catholic Ormonde Boys, fought street battles.
sections.crises:
In 1315 a Scottish army under Edward the Bruce burned the city's suburbs. The Black Death reached Dublin in 1348 and killed thousands over the following decade; the plague recurred regularly until its last major outbreak in 1649. A plague from 1649 to 1651 wiped out almost half of the city's inhabitants. In the Nine Years War of the 1590s English soldiers were housed by the townsmen of Dublin and spread disease, and the English Army's gunpowder store on Winetavern Street exploded accidentally in 1597, killing nearly 200 Dubliners. The city was besieged twice during the Irish Confederate Wars, in 1646 and 1649, and on both occasions the attackers were driven off. In 1649 the Parliamentarian garrison routed a mixed Irish Confederate and Royalist force at the Battle of Rathmines.

After the Act of Union of 1800 the city lost the income that came with parliament and the viceregal court, and many Georgian mansions were put up for sale and became slums. Robert Emmet's one-day rebellion of 1803 was put down. In 1913 the Lockout, a labour dispute between the Irish Transport and General Workers Union and employers led by William Martin Murphy, left 25,000 workers on strike or locked out within a month, and rioting left three people dead. In the Easter Rising of 1916 much of the city centre was destroyed by shell fire, and around 450 people, about half of them civilians, were killed. Fighting at the start of the Civil War in 1922 and the burning of the Custom House in 1921 destroyed more of the city's buildings. A German bombing on 31 May 1941 killed 34 civilians in the North Strand.
sections.legacy:
Much of Dublin's architecture and layout dates from the Georgian period, and some medieval streets around Temple Bar, Aungier Street, Capel Street and Thomas Street were less affected by the rebuilding. Dublin Castle, Christ Church Cathedral and St Patrick's Cathedral date from the Anglo-Norman city. Trinity College holds the Book of Kells, an illustrated manuscript created by Irish monks around 800 CE. After the Free State rebuilt the centre, Parliament was set up in Leinster House, where it has remained.

Large parts of Georgian Dublin were demolished or substantially redeveloped in the mid-20th century, and Wood Quay, where the oldest remains of Viking Dublin lay, was built over with the headquarters of the city's local government after a long planning struggle. Nelson's Pillar in O'Connell Street was blown up in 1966, and the Spire of Dublin was erected on the spot in 2003. From the 1980s planners worked to preserve the Georgian neighbourhoods and Temple Bar, the last part of the city with its original medieval street plan.

Dublin has a long literary history, and it produced the Nobel laureates William Butler Yeats, George Bernard Shaw and Samuel Beckett, and writers such as Jonathan Swift, Oscar Wilde, Bram Stoker and James Joyce, whose Ulysses is set in the city. The Abbey Theatre was founded in 1904. In the 2022 census the city, including its suburbs, had a population of 1,263,219.

summary: Dublin began as a Viking fortified base of about 841 on the Liffey and became the seat of Anglo-Norman and English power in Ireland, with a castle from 1204. It was rebuilt as a Georgian city, lost its parliament in 1800, and became the capital of the Irish Free State in 1922.
references: David Dickson, Dublin The Making of a Capital City (Profile Books Ltd., 2014)
Constantia Maxwell, Dublin Under the Georges (Lambay Books, 1997)
notes: START: 841 (the Vikings' fortified base, 'Viking settlement of about 841') with circa true. The main article also says the Irish government recognised 988 as the year of settlement; the history article says 988 'might not have been accurate' (the Norse king recognised Máel Sechnaill II, who captured the city in 989). I give 988 only as the government's recognition in facts.founded and origins, and left the 989 point out.
PTOLEMY / Eblana: main article says 'possibly the earliest reference'; history article says doubt has been cast and the similarity is thought coincidental. I gave both views.
BLACK MONDAY 1209: main article does not mention it; history article names the O'Byrnes in one place and the O'Toole clan in another. Left out entirely.

END OF VIKING RULE: the main article says Norman invasion launched in 1169 and Strongbow gained control; the history article says Diarmait captured the city in 1171 and the Norse king Ascall was beheaded on 16 May 1171. I wrote 'until 1169' for Viking control (main article) and gave 1171 only for Henry II's invasion and the Anglo-Norman takeover as the history article says; the sequence of who took Dublin in which year is not fully reconciled, so the editor should read origins/rulers.

POPULATION c. 1700: main article says over 50,000 by 1700; the history article says over 60,000 by 1700 and second largest city in the British Empire after London. The main article says the Georgian city was briefly second-largest in the Empire with over 130,000. I used 50,000 only and left out the second-largest claim.
13th-century population: 8,000 (main article) against 5,000 to 10,000 for the medieval city (history article); both given, with different wording.

EASTER RISING dead: only the history article gives figures: about 450 killed in the account of the Rising and 482 in the later summary of the revolutionary period. I used 'around 450' as the Rising paragraph gives it.
PLAGUE 1649: the history article says the plague 'recurred regularly until its last major outbreak in 1649'; the main article says a plague from 1649 to 1651 wiped out almost half. Both kept.
DUBLIN AND MONAGHAN BOMBINGS: the articles give 34 (main) and 33 (history) dead; I did not use the event.
The 'Blackpitts' mass graves are disputed in the history article (tanning pits); left out. 'Dublin was briefly the second-largest city in the British Empire' left out as above.

Left out: tourism, transport, sport, economy and present government, as the brief asks. The 2022 population figure is given without the 'as of' wording; the main article gives the city council area as 592,713 or 592,713 in different places, so only the city-with-suburbs figure is used (the two articles also give the county figure differently).
'Dublin became the capital of the Irish Free State' in 1922: main article says 1922; the history article says the Free State was proclaimed on 6 December 1922 and elsewhere 'by 1923'. 1922 used.
